Colloque à Tunis | Les causes de l’infertilité et les moyens d’y remédier
items.description: Les difficultés à procréer sont un phénomène croissant au sein de la société tunisienne, a indiqué le président de la Société tunisienne de gynécologie-obstétrique (STGO) et chef du service de gynécologie-obstétrique de Bizerte, Mechaal Mourali, lors des travaux des 5 èmes Journées de la médecine reproductive, consacrées au traitement de l’infertilité et au recul de l’âge de la procréation, qui se tiennent les 19 et 20 septembre 2026 à Gammarth, au nord de Tunis, sous l’égide de la STGO. Dr Mourali attribue cette évolution à plusieurs facteurs, notamment la pollution et le mode de vie, ainsi que le stress, la sédentarité, l’obésité, le tabagisme et la consommation d’alcool et de drogues. Ces facteurs peuvent affecter la fertilité tant chez l’homme que chez la femme — en altérant la qualité des spermatozoïdes ou des ovocytes — et ainsi accroître les difficultés de procréation, a souligné le praticien, en expliquant que l’amélioration de la fertilité ne dépend pas uniquement des techniques médicales modernes, mais commence également par une modification du mode de vie — notamment la pratique d’une activité physique, la réduction du stress et l’arrêt du tabac — autant de facteurs susceptibles d’accroître les chances de conception. Les progrès des techniques de procréation assistée ont également contribué à améliorer les taux de réussite, a aussi indiqué Dr Mourali, tout en évoquant le rôle que peut jouer l’intelligence artificielle pour aider les médecins et les couples à choisir les meilleures options thérapeutiques, y compris pour l’évaluation et la sélection des spermatozoïdes et des ovocytes les plus appropriés. Le colloque a également abordé le rôle de la chirurgie dans le traitement de certaines causes de difficultés de procréation. Certaines interventions chirurgicales peuvent en effet contribuer à améliorer la fertilité et à traiter divers problèmes rencontrés par les femmes. Dr Mourali a insisté sur le fait que la combinaison de changements de mode de vie, de techniques modernes et, si nécessaire, de la chirurgie, offre de multiples options thérapeutiques pour faire face aux difficultés de procréation. I. B. L’article Colloque à Tunis | Les causes de l’infertilité et les moyens d’y remédier est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Coalition defends NSCDC chief over Minna deaths
items.description: Rejects calls for Audi’s removal, urges probe to run its course The Centre for Justice for Common Nigeria, under the Coalition of Nigerian Civil Society Organisations, has rejected calls for the removal of the Commandant-General of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), Professor Ahmed Abubakar Audi, over the deaths of 37 suspected illegal miners in the Corps’ custody in Minna, Niger State. The coalition, in a statement responding to a call by lawyer and human rights activist Hamza N. Dantani for the termination of Audi’s tenure, described the demand as premature and argued that responsibility should be established through investigation and due process rather than public pressure. It said the deaths were a grave matter that required justice for the deceased and their families, but argued that accountability should be based on evidence identifying those directly responsible for the incident. The coalition maintained that Audi did not order the enforcement operation, was not present during the arrests and, according to its account, had no prior knowledge of the circumstances surrounding the deaths. The suspects were arrested during NSCDC operations conducted in parts of Niger State on September 15 and 16, 2026. The Niger State Commandant, Suberu Siyaka Aniviye, was subsequently suspended pending investigation. According to the coalition, the operations were carried out under the Niger State Command and should therefore not automatically be attributed to the national leadership of the Corps. It argued that the NSCDC operates through a hierarchical command structure in which state commands have responsibility for day-to-day enforcement operations within their jurisdictions. The coalition also said Audi responded to the incident by ordering an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the deaths. It noted that the Federal Government has since taken additional steps, including suspending 20 other NSCDC personnel linked to the incident and constituting a 10-member independent committee to investigate the deaths and determine responsibility. The committee, constituted by Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo following President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s directive for a comprehensive and transparent investigation, has two weeks to complete its assignment and submit its report. The coalition said the investigative process should be allowed to establish whether there were acts of negligence, misconduct or other violations and identify those responsible before sanctions are imposed. It also argued that removing Audi before the conclusion of the investigation could amount to prejudging the matter. The coalition invoked the principle of presumption of innocence, saying that a public official should not be treated as personally culpable merely because a serious incident occurred within an institution under his leadership. It said no evidence had been presented linking Audi personally to the deaths or showing that he ordered, authorised or had prior knowledge of any unlawful conduct relating to the detainees. The group further argued that accountability should follow the chain of responsibility and be directed at individuals whose actions or omissions are established by evidence to have contributed to the incident. It listed the suspension of the Niger State commandant and other personnel, the Federal Government’s independent investigation and separate investigative efforts by security agencies as evidence that accountability mechanisms were already in motion. The coalition warned against what it described as scapegoating senior officials before facts had been established. It said the priority should be to determine what happened to the detainees, establish the causes of death and identify anyone whose conduct contributed to the tragedy. The coalition also called on the Federal Government to ensure that the 10-member committee operates independently and that its findings are made public. It urged the NSCDC leadership to cooperate fully with the investigation and implement any reforms required to prevent a recurrence. The group appealed to activists and other stakeholders to focus on ensuring a thorough and transparent investigation rather than demanding the removal of officials before the process is concluded. The deaths have generated public outrage and prompted protests in Minna, with the Federal Government suspending personnel and ordering an independent investigation. The actual circumstances and causes of the deaths remain subject to investigation. The coalition said the families of the deceased deserved answers and justice, but maintained that those found responsible should be sanctioned on the basis of evidence and due process. items.title: Carburants en France : Le prix du gazole franchit la barre record de 2,41 euros le litre
items.description: Le prix du gazole en France a atteint 2,41 euros en moyenne, dimanche, un nouveau record en pleine crise géopolitique où les approvisionnements sont fortement perturbés. Dans le détail, le prix du litre de gazole atteint 2,4097 euros, selon une moyenne calculée par les analystes et rapportée par les médias français à partir des prix affichés dimanche pour plus de 8.700 stations-service, dépassant ainsi le record établi la veille. Le SP95-E10, carburant le plus vendu en France, évolue depuis plus d'une dizaine de jours au-dessus de son pic de 2022, relève la même source, ajoutant que le SP98 dépasse, quant à lui, 2,28 euros en moyenne, selon une moyenne enregistrée dans plus de 6.800 stations. La flambée des prix du carburant depuis fin février provoquée par la guerre en Iran alimente une tension sociale déjà matérialisée jeudi par des blocages de dépôt pétroliers par des pêcheurs en Méditerranée. Toutes les stations n'actualisent pas quotidiennement leurs tarifs. Pour le calcul de la moyenne, l’analyse a été basée sur les stations ayant renseigné un prix sur le site gouvernemental il y a moins de 31 jours. Ce délai est rallongé quand le prix paraît volontairement plafonné, comme cela est pratiqué par les stations TotalEnergies, indique-t-on. items.title: PTI says Aleema detained by authorities as Lahore DC orders arrest under MPO
items.description: The PTI said on Sunday that ex-prime minister and PTI founder Imran Khan’s sister, Aleema Khan, had been detained by authorities while an order issued by the office of Lahore’s deputy commissioner confirmed that he had ordered their detention or arrest for a period of 30 days. The Sept 20 order, a copy of which is available with Dawn , said Deputy Commissioner (DC) Muhammad Ali Ijaz had ordered their detention or arrest under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, 1960 (MPO). The MPO allows the authorities to order detention and restrict judicial review of such orders. The DC also directed the arrest of a Muhammad Ameer in his order, adding, “Their custody shall be placed under the superintendent, Central Jail, Kot Lakhpat, Lahore. They shall be at liberty to make a representation to the provincial government against this order.” In his order, the DC cited a letter by the Lahore capital city police officer. The order stated that the letter referred to police reports that said Aleema and Ameer “are prejudicial to the public safety and maintenance of public order”. The reports also mentioned that the two had been involved in roadblocks and protests on May 9, 2023, when PTI supporters and workers took to the streets against Imran’s arrest. “They motivated the workers to damage public and government property. Moreover, they are again mobilising the workers through social media and public meetings to create law and order situation, raising/chanting objectionable slogans amongst the general public against the government/institution in order to provoke and incite them,” the order read. It said multiple cases had been registered against the two. declaring them “potential dangers to public peace and tranquility”. According to the order, the Civil Lines Division superintendent of police and district intelligence branch in-charge recommended their detention under the MPO for a 30-day period “in order to keep the law and order situation in the city intact”. Dawn has reached out to police for a comment but there has been no immediate response. Meanwhile, PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan posted on X that he had been informed about Aleema’s “arrest” by her sister, Noreen Niazi. The development takes place amid reports of a crackdown on the PTI ahead of its Sept 27 protest, which the party has called to demand Imran’s release from jail and mobilise people for the supremacy of the Constitution. In his post, Gohar said, “We have clarified that our protest will be peaceful. Our objective is to peacefully struggle for the fulfilment of our constitutional and political demands; we don’t want any kind of clash or violence. “Arresting Aleema Khan sahiba under the MPO in this situation is tantamount to fuelling violence and tension. We strongly condemn it.” He called for an end to all such actions and demanded Aleema’s immediate release. The party would soon present its strategy against such actions, he said. Earlier, the PTI posted on X that Aleema had been “abducted” in Lahore from outside her home by the authorities. PTI Central Information Secretary Sheikh Waqas Akram also demanded in a post on X that Aleema be presented in court immediately. “A sister is being punished for speaking up for her brother,” Akram alleged. In a statement, the PTI termed Aleema’s “arrest” a “cowardly and deliberate attempt to worsen the situation”. Meanwhile, opposition alliance Tehreek-i-Tahaffuz Ayeen-i-Pakistan (TTAP) also condemned the arrest in a statement. The statement said the move was tantamount crossing all limits of “state oppression and political revenge. “The TTAP strong condemns this step by the government, especially the Punjab government. This action exposes the Punjab government’s current oppressive system,” it added. The opposition alliance said Aleema’s arrest would not be tolerated and demanded her immediate release. “The Punjab government must realise that oppression, arrests and revengeful acts cannot resolve political differences,” the TTAP said, reiterating its demand for Aleema’s release, as well as that of other “political prisoners”. Aleema’s arrest follow a string of reported actions against the PTI in Punjab ahead of its Sept 27 protest. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi alleged during his visit to Punjab last week that he had “ abducted ” by authorities in Lahore and later “thrown” by the roadside. He also claimed a man had been sent to kill him. The Punjab government had swiftly refuted the claims of arrest, while the Wazirabad police clarified that the man accused by Afridi was a police constable deployed on security duty for the CM. Earlier, district authorities had also issued preventive detention orders against dozens of PTI workers under Section 3 of the Maintenance of Public Order, including 31 in one Punjab notification and a further 14 in Toba Tek Singh. Similar reports have come from Islamabad, to where the PTI plans to march on Sept 27. But, the government has vowed to stop the march and the Islamabad High Court has ruled that no political party or its leadership has the “lawful right to occupy public roads, highways, interchanges, toll plazas and buildings in Islamabad”. On Saturday, the capital police took into custody four PTI activists and workers. A police officer told Dawn the activists were arrested under separate charges in response to a complaint lodged by a sub-inspector. The police got information that the PTI workers were holding a meeting in connection with the Sep 27 protest at a property dealer’s office in the area of E-16. A police team was constituted for the raid and the arrest. The police claimed that the workers tortured the police team when they raided the meeting venue, besides, tearing their uniform and taking them hostage. Officers in the police and capital administration said that they have started preparations to counter the PTI’s countrywide protest. Last week, PTI Secretary General Salman Akram Raja said he was “released” after being briefly detained, with the PTI claiming he was held by Islamabad police. Authorities have also placed hundreds of containers at the city’s entry points as the administration braces for protests.

items.title: TTAP forms committee to consult with political parties, reach consensus on all-parties moot
items.description: The Tehreek-i-Tahafuz Ayeen-i-Pakistan (TTAP) on Sunday formed a six-member committee to hold consultations with political parties and reach an agreement on the agenda for a proposed multi-party conference. The opposition had announced the proposed moot earlier this month. In a post on social media platform X, the opposition alliance announced the formation of the six-member committee, which will include: Leader of the Opposition in the Senate Allama Raja Nasir Abbas Jafri; PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Khan; TTAP’s Secretary General Asad Qaiser; Vice Chairman Mustafa Nawaz Khokhar; spokesperson Akhwanzada Hussain Ahmed Yousafzai; and PTI Core Committee member Khalid Yousaf Chaudhry. According to the statement, the committee will liaise with other political parties regarding the proposed moot, consult them on its agenda and work towards reaching agreement on the way forward. The notification said the committee would continue its consultation and coordination process under the guidance of the TTAP leadership. On Sept 11, the opposition announced it intended to hold consultations to call an all-parties conference to discuss several issues, including the creation of new provinces, law and order and the economy. At the time, Barrister Gohar, speaking to the media after a meeting of his party with Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F), had outlined plans to hold an all-parties conference, saying that “the current law and order situation, the economy, inflation, lawlessness, and the creation of new provinces issue” called for such measures.

items.description: TEHRAN- The new Indian ambassador to Iran, at the start of his mission, visited the Tehran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture (TCCIMA) and met with the chairman of the Chamber. items.title: Shatta Wale challenges UPSA students to build entrepreneurial mindsets
items.description: Ghanaian musician and entrepreneur Charles Nii Armah Mensah Jr., popularly known as Shatta Wale, has challenged students of the University of Professional Studies, Accra (UPSA) to cultivate entrepreneurial mindsets to ensure their success. The award-winning artiste urged young people to look beyond academic qualifications and focus on developing the mindset needed to identify and seize opportunities in an increasingly competitive world. Shatta Wale said this while addressing students at the UPSA 1000 and Ghana Entrepreneurship Conference. The event formed part of the University’s entrepreneurship and mentorship initiative aimed at exposing students to practical industry experiences, leadership insights and entrepreneurial opportunities. The programme brings together accomplished professionals, business executives and innovators to inspire students and prepare them for the world of work and enterprise development. “The deepest part of my journey isn’t the song, it isn’t the crowd, it isn’t even one particular business. It is the mind that keeps evolving,” Shatta Wale said. He encouraged students not to imitate his lifestyle or public persona but rather learn from his way of thinking, adaptability and determination. “Don’t copy my life. What I would rather let you copy is my thinking,” he stated, stressing that personal growth and success were rooted in discipline, self-belief and lifelong learning. The musician, who has built a career spanning music production, digital content distribution, and entrepreneurship, shared insights into how he leveraged technology and online platforms to generate income and expand his brand beyond entertainment. He noted that many young people were yet to fully appreciate the opportunities available through technology and the digital economy. “Success begins with vision and preparation. You have to see it before everybody sees it and believe it before everybody believes it. When you don’t see yourself as the next chartered accountant or the next billionaire, nobody will see it for you,” he added. The artiste urged the students to transform challenges into opportunities by developing problem-solving skills, investing wisely and continuously upgrading their knowledge. He advised them to turn “problems into questions, questions into ideas, ideas into actions, income into assets and success into another opportunity.” Shatta Wale cautioned against complacency, saying that achieving financial success should not mark the end of personal ambition and growth. “Don’t let success make your mind lazy. Keep learning, keep asking, keep building and keep evolving because a powerful mind is not a mind that knows everything; it is a mind that refuses to stop learning,” he said. He emphasised that before building wealth or businesses, young people must first develop the capacity to manage and sustain them. “Before you build the money, build the mind that can manage the money. Before you build the business, build the mind that can lead the business. Before you build the empire, build the mind that won’t destroy the empire,” he advised. Born Charles Nii Armah Mensah Jr., Shatta Wale is one of Ghana’s most influential music personalities and entrepreneurs. Over the years, he has built a strong brand in the entertainment industry while expanding into business ventures and digital enterprises, earning recognition for his resilience, reinvention and entrepreneurial approach to career development.

items.title: Burkina/ Hakili Mousso 2026 : L'excellence scientifique féminine à l'honneur
items.description: Le Premier ministre Rimtalba Jean Emmanuel Ouédraogo a présidé, le samedi 19 septembre 2026 à Ouagadougou, la cérémonie de distinction des lauréates de la première édition du concours national Hakili Mousso. L'information est rapportée par la Primature du Burkina Faso. Cette initiative vise à promouvoir l'excellence scientifique féminine et à encourager les jeunes filles à s'engager dans les disciplines scientifiques. Ouvert aux bachelières de la session 2026, le concours a porté sur les mathématiques, la physique et la chimie. En chimie, Inès Nikiema a remporté le premier prix avec 18,73/20, tandis qu'Aminata Traoré s'est classée première en physique avec 15/20. En mathématiques, Adjaratou Bama a obtenu la première place avec 14,25/20. C'est après les sélections régionales que 84 candidates ont pris part à la finale nationale, à l'issue de laquelle cinq prix ont été attribués dans chacune des trois disciplines, avec notamment des récompenses financières, des motos, des ordinateurs, des bourses et des bons de carburant. La cérémonie a également mis en lumière la sous-représentation des filles dans les filières scientifiques. Selon les données présentées, elles représentaient 36,7% des effectifs des filières scientifiques en 2025-2026, contre 59,5% dans les filières non scientifiques. Le concours est ainsi présenté comme un moyen d'encourager davantage de jeunes filles à s'orienter vers les sciences, les technologies et les domaines industriels. Le Premier ministre a également souligné le rôle des enseignants et des parents dans l'accompagnement des jeunes filles et a appelé les lauréates à poursuivre leur engagement dans les domaines scientifiques. Les lauréates ont pour leur part, pris l'engagement de devenir des ambassadrices de la science et de mettre leurs compétences au service du Burkina Faso. Lefaso.net Source : Primature du Burkina Faso

items.title: The Pinball President
items.description: In 1946, the year that Donald Trump was born, the pinball machine offered everything but control. The bumpers were propulsive, the lights flashed, but the player’s only honest move was to pull a spring-loaded plunger. After that, the ball belonged to the machine, zinging and zooming wherever the bumpers sent it. This is how many Americans experience the Trump presidency today: antic caroming that they can do little more than watch. The ballroom. The Iran war. The threats against Canada. Greenland. Portraits of himself as Christ, a decorated general, or the pope. The arch. The Kennedy Center. Prosecution of enemies. Pardons. Imaginary Reflecting Pool vandals. Federal incursions into voting. Tariffs on. Tariffs off. Tariffs on again. The Qatari plane. Endless promises—to release tax returns, to end corruption, to deliver $5,000 checks—that never materialize. No president has been more with us than Trump, because no president has been better at seizing public attention. But there is a difference between getting attention and doing something with it. For months, the president has been unable to convince the public that he’s up to the job. In a CNN poll released at the end of July, 65 percent of respondents said that his policies had worsened the economy, and only 28 percent approved of his handling of Iran. Voters have watched the caroming and have concluded that he doesn’t have his eye on the ball. They care about the economy, and he seems to care about everything else. Only 27 percent of adults told CNN that Trump has the right priorities, down from 45 percent when the term began. And a record 73 percent said he hasn’t paid enough attention to the country’s most important issues. In June, while Trump was fixated on the Reflecting Pool and stopping widespread voter fraud that doesn’t exist, a bipartisan housing bill aimed at high costs reached his desk. He called it “a big yawn” and said he hadn’t decided whether to sign it. In July, he let it become law without his signature. This is a problem for Republicans in November 2026, but it’s an opportunity for voters looking to November 2028. Once a roster of candidates emerges, their supporters will discover that the office demands—wouldn’t you know it?—exactly the qualities that their preferred candidate happens to possess. Now, when there’s no one horse to back, is the time to use the current president’s rat-a-tat treatment of our attention to ask how we want the next president to spend it. Many voters will ask only one thing of the next president: Don’t be Donald Trump . Fair enough. But stopping at “not Trump” wastes the extremity of the Trump years. Extremes clarify. A flood shows you where the ground was always low. The Trump years have been a reminder that the presidency is a trust. The public’s attention belongs to the public. A president borrows it, and the test at every turn is whether he spends it on their account or his own. Trump treats it as a possession, to do with as he pleases, like the East Wing. For him, the public is his cheering section. A president who ignores the half of the country that voted against him teaches them that elections are conquests. They will remember that when they win. [ Ashley Parker and Michael Scherer: ‘I run the country and the world’ ] It’s true that when Trump wants to focus the nation’s attention on something, he is relentless: immigration, his enemies, his ballroom. In April, The Washington Post found that he had publicly mentioned the ballroom on roughly a third of the days by that point in the year; he had posted about it more than about tariffs. But what he cares about often isn’t in the nation’s greater interest. A trustee doesn’t spend the trust on himself. The next president should ration his calls on the public’s attention, which, after all, protects his own effectiveness and the country’s. “Public psychology,” Franklin Roosevelt wrote in 1935 to a reporter urging him to speak out more often, “cannot, because of human weakness, be attuned for long periods of time to a constant repetition of the highest note in the scale.” When Roosevelt did speak, he explained. In his first fireside chat, he walked the country through how a bank works. Explanation is what lets a president speak less: A public that has been shown why can carry the argument on its own, and a public that has only been told what must be told again tomorrow. A president cannot push opinion where it doesn’t want to go, only nudge it, and that is possible only if he hasn’t already worn the audience out. A president who is always talking cannot use talking to signal that this time matters . The creed of this current era is the opposite. “If you’re not making news, you’re not governing,” wrote former Representative Matt Gaetz, who made news nearly every day he served and governed not at all. A president who consumes the country’s attention spends down a resource that citizens need for their own affairs, including those delightful corners of human experience that should be free of political consideration. The UFC fighter Bryce Mitchell understood this before the bouts on the White House lawn this summer. Mitchell, who did not participate, said that the government was “desecrating its role in society.” The government, he said, “is supposed to protect us, not entertain us.” Sometimes a president doesn’t have to ask for the country’s attention, because catastrophe has already gathered it. In these cases, a president can act as a moral force, particularly in consolation. Reagan after the Challenger explosion, Clinton after the Oklahoma City bombing, the younger Bush after the attacks of 9/11, and Obama at Emanuel AME in Charleston, South Carolina. Each president spent the nation’s attention on its grief and, in doing so, reminded the nation what it valued. Trump has nearly erased this part of the job, inventing a new one in its place: chief grave dancer. When Rob Reiner was murdered in December, Trump blamed Reiner himself; when Robert Mueller died in March, Trump wrote , “Good, I’m glad he’s dead.” A president sends a moral signal not just in the words he uses but also in what he chooses to spend them on. After the white-nationalist march and the death of Heather Heyer in Charlottesville, Virginia, in August 2017, Trump denounced the Nazis, but the thrust of his attention was aimed elsewhere. He obsessed over the counterprotesters. He praised himself for being the only one brave enough to name what he claimed were the misdeeds of the people opposing the Nazis. “You had a group on one side that was bad, and you had a group on the other side that was also very violent,” he insisted without evidence, “and nobody wants to say it, but I will say it right now.” He sent six tweets about Charlottesville and, in those tweets, never used the terms racism , bigotry , or white nationalism . He sent 37 tweets about NFL players kneeling during the anthem. All of this happens where we can see it. We tend to treat the presidency as if it existed only in that public form. Most of it doesn’t. Because much of the job happens in secret or out of camera range, what the president chooses to do with public attention is our best evidence of how he sorts the world in private. That evidence has limits. A president who never mentions the deficit might be working on it every morning. Eisenhower’s style was called the “hidden hand”: The president who looked idle at the podium was working the levers out of sight. But a president whose public attention shows no discipline, discernment, or patience isn’t going to discover those attributes at the necessary scale when the cameras turn away. Trump governs by the Heisman hand, always in your face. [ George T. Conway III: Unfit for office ] The presidency demands brutal prioritization. “I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important,” goes a line that Eisenhower liked to quote . “The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent.” It was such a simple idea that it became the Eisenhower Matrix, used by managers everywhere to sort incoming challenges. The principle applies with more force in a job where the urgent arrives by the hour. If missile stockpiles are low, we want a president fixing that now, not giving a speech about the deficit. But we also want a president who can see the deficit coming and feel some obligation to the future citizens who will live under galactic debt. Trump spends a lot of his time on matters that are neither important nor urgent. The New York Times reporter Maggie Haberman, who has covered Trump for 30 years, has said that if you charted his mind these days, 70 percent of it would go to gilding, construction, renaming, and tribute projects. The exhaustion after Trump will produce an appetite for quiet. It has happened before. George W. Bush campaigned on restoring dignity to the office because Americans were worn out by the dramas of the Clinton years; he wanted a presidency that his team promised would show up on page A24 of the newspaper. But quiet is not a standard. The office needs a benchmark built from the job itself, not from the last man to hold it. Nor should the next president react to Trump’s frivolity by turning every subject into a family talk in the living room about Important Matters—a brittle standard where partisans adopt the posture of the online scold who answers “I love dogs” with “Your silence on cats is deafening.” Under that standard, a president must speak to everything, and a president who speaks to everything has no time left to do anything. Campaigns often measure for qualities that have little or nothing to do with the office. But voters can evaluate how candidates treat public attention on the campaign trail and make some inferences about how they would approach the job. Here are some questions to ask: Does the candidate choose problems that a president can actually move, and can he say why those and not others? Can a president articulate a vision for the country to people who are not likely to vote for her? Can he explain rather than merely assert? Does she ever talk about a problem that won’t pay off before the next election? Can he let a news cycle pass without joining it? And when grief or outrage arrives, does he show any evidence of a concern for the entire nation? How a candidate handles these moments during a campaign—when public attention, ever more scarce in the age of the algorithm, is the only thing he has to spend—tells us how that candidate will spend ours. In 1947, the year after Trump’s birth, pinball changed. The flipper was added, which meant the player was no longer merely watching. Where the ball went was now, at least in part, up to the player. In 2028, voters will be in the game again. But that requires attention to the office now.

items.title: A Show That Lovingly Pokes Fun at Gen Z
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. Welcome back to The Daily’s Sunday culture edition, in which one Atlantic writer or editor reveals what’s keeping them entertained. Today’s special guest is Emma Williams, an associate editor who helps oversee the magazine’s social media and has also written about her home state of Texas . Emma is a habitual rewatcher of Normal People , a show that she says has resonated with her differently over time. She also enjoys listening to her namesake Emmylou Harris, laughing over Adults episodes, and watching Hailee Catalano’s comforting cooking videos. — Stephanie Bai, senior associate editor The television show I’m most enjoying right now: The first scene of FX’s Adults tells you pretty much everything you need to know about the show: It’s crass, crude, absurd, and indulgently hilarious . Adults pokes fun at Gen Z without being judgmental or predictable, and it features some familiarly ridiculous plights. Maybe don’t watch it with your grandmother—but your spunky aunt is probably okay. A quiet song that I love: I discovered the British DJ Fred Again when I was going down an NPR Tiny Desk Concert rabbit hole years ago. I was immediately struck by his talent—but over time, I have come to better appreciate the emotion he evokes through his performances. Even in his natural habitat, behind the DJ booth, Fred isn’t what you might normally expect from an EDM artist: He samples spoken-word poems, Zoom calls, and random internet videos to create songs that you can just as easily dance to as you can cry to. I know I’m cheating a bit by saying that his entire Tiny Desk production is my favorite quiet song, but the fact that he was able to pull off an acoustic EDM performance is remarkable. To re-create the sound of electronic beats, he used the marimba, the vibraphone, and the piano; he also pounded and tapped on a desk and layered in his soft, husky voice. It is gentle, engrossing, and stupidly impressive. A loud song that I love: The first time I heard “Dance Yrself Clean,” by LCD Soundsystem, I was confused. My best friend played it for me, and by minute two, I was enjoying the song, but I could not comprehend how this hazy and somewhat repetitive tune could continue for another seven minutes and be as “life changing” as she had promised. Then I hit 3:05 on the track. I felt the ba-da-da-dum in my bones before James Murphy’s newly impassioned voice flooded through the speakers. This is now my song for any moment when I need to drown out my thoughts. Whether I’m going through a breakup, a bad day, or an existential crisis, I’ll put on “Dance Yrself Clean” and itch through the first three minutes, eagerly anticipating the rush of euphoria that hits after the beat drops. Years later, that same friend and I heard the song live. I have no idea whether we were crying or laughing or shouting, but I know we were dancing with abandon—and letting the music wash over us. A cultural product I loved as a teenager and still love: I watched Normal People for the first time when I was 19, and I’ve rewatched it at least once a year every year since. I have never wavered in my fondness for it, but my reaction to the characters and storylines has evolved with time. When I first saw the show, based on Sally Rooney’s novel of the same name, I fell madly in love with Connell, barely registering that his cold avoidance of Marianne in public was wrong. I just thought he was broody and complicated; therefore, to my teenage mind, he was perfect and dreamy. I’m glad to say that I have moved past that (kind of), and I now find it difficult to watch his treatment of Marianne in the first few episodes. In my 20s, I resonate more with Marianne’s college arc. Specifically, her need to become the coolest, most stylish, most successful version of herself—even if it comes at the cost of her own happiness. Marianne and Connell’s lack of clear communication is always maddening. But I understand it more with age. Sometimes vocalizing what you really want can be more terrifying than staying quiet. A musical artist who means a lot to me: I have to pay homage to my namesake, the inimitable country folk artist Emmylou Harris. Her music reminds me of my home state of Texas. Listening to her song “Boulder to Birmingham” transports me back to long drives through the plains of West Texas and the seemingly endless miles of wind turbines. I hear my parents’ voices, lovingly calling me Emmylou and Emmy-lou-lou. Whenever I feel adrift, her music pulls me back to the ground. A YouTuber, TikToker, Twitch streamer, or other online creator I’m a fan of: I have an embarrassing confession: There is a cooking influencer whom I’m really obsessed with—as in, I went to a meet and greet of hers, and I send her the occasional tipsy Instagram DM. (Sometimes she even responds!) Hailee Catalano is a James Beard–winning chef. Her food is fresh and unique, and her video style isn’t gimmicky or aggressive like that of so many other cooking accounts—it’s simple and personable. My favorite series of hers is called Friday Night Dinner , which is a collaboration with her partner, Chuck Cruz, who is also a chef and content creator. They film themselves making a new meal every week, and I can only describe their vibe as homey. The videos sometimes have awkward pauses and funny asides (and, of course, clips of their dog, Gus), and watching them makes me feel like I’m sitting at the kitchen counter as two of my friends prepare something delicious for us to eat. A poem, or line of poetry, that I return to: The older I get, the more I find myself recalling the lines of Langston Hughes’s poem “ Harlem .” Hughes asks: “What happens to a dream deferred?” I recently turned 25, and the “quarter-life crisis” is certainly hitting me. I think about all of my childhood hopes that have dissipated, and all of the ones I still have that I’m not sure will come true. I, too, wonder what happens to these dreams. Here are three Sunday reads from The Atlantic : George Packer on sons and mothers Anne Applebaum: MAGA is making the world safe for corruption. What comes after America The Week Ahead Primetime , a crime thriller about the rise of the To Catch a Predator host Chris Hansen and the world of televised vigilantism (in theaters Friday) Youth , a comedic-drama series about a 50-year-old divorcée balancing dating with caring for her aging parents and adult son (streaming today on HBO Max) Mazywood , a horror novel by Tananarive Due about a man uncovering the truth about his grandmother, set in Old Hollywood and the present day (out Tuesday) Essay Illustration by Alisa Gao / The Atlantic Math Can’t Go On Like This By Kai Williams In late July, one of the world’s most famous mathematicians issued a warning to his field. Math is entering a “turbulent period,” the UCLA professor Terence Tao said in front of a packed lecture hall at the International Congress of Mathematicians. AI is getting so good at math, he said, that it’s causing a “crisis in our mathematical values and practices.” Earlier in the same week that Tao gave his talk at math’s most prestigious conference, a researcher at Anthropic had used Claude to disprove an 87-year-old math conjecture. Still, when I asked mathematicians at the conference about their experiences with AI, most hadn’t thought deeply about the topic. Many seemed a little surprised that a journalist was asking them about it at all. Read the full article.
